record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: Is it possible to decouple search efficiency from peer autonomy in a data-sharing peer-to-peer system, so that peers retain substantial control over topology, data placement, and routing-related choices without sacrificing efficient search?

evidence.quote: Decoupling efficiency from autonomy seems to be the greatest challenge, since existing techniques almost uniformly sacrifice autonomy to achieve efficiency.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a data-sharing peer-to-peer system modeled as a dynamic distributed network of autonomous nodes (peers), where each peer independently controls: (i) its local choice of neighbors in the overlay topology, (ii) the placement of data items it stores or replicates, and (iii) the routing and forwarding decisions it makes for queries (including which queries to forward, to whom, and how to index content). A search operation takes as input a query (e.g., a keyword or key) issued at some peer, and must locate peers holding data items matching the query. Say that a search protocol is efficient if, in expectation over random query origins and content distributions consistent with peers' autonomous choices, the number of messages and the latency required to answer a query are polylogarithmic in the number of peers n, and that it preserves peer autonomy if no peer is required to surrender control over (i), (ii), or (iii) to a global scheme (i.e., each peer's choices in these three dimensions may be made according to its own local policies, subject only to mild local constraints).

Question: Does there exist a search protocol for such a peer-to-peer system that is simultaneously efficient and autonomy-preserving in the above sense? Equivalently, can search efficiency be decoupled from peer autonomy, so that peers retain substantial control over topology, data placement, and routing choices without sacrificing polylogarithmic-cost search?
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface a definitive resolution to the general question of decoupling search efficiency from peer autonomy in unstructured/autonomous P2P systems. Subsequent work on hybrid, semantic, and unstructured overlays (e.g., semantic overlay networks, gossip-based search, hybrid DHT systems) offers partial trade-offs but no proof that full autonomy and polylogarithmic-cost search can be achieved simultaneously in general. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Semantic Overlay Networks for P2P Systems
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes semantic overlays that preserve peer autonomy while improving search efficiency, but trade-offs remain.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress: heuristic improvements without a general efficiency-autonomy decoupling result.
